title: Step 11: Background jobs: job table + SKIP LOCKED + a Go worker pool, with graceful shutdown
summary: Work that must survive restarts is a row in a jobs table: SKIP LOCKED hands each job to one worker, a lease returns a dead worker's job, run_after spaces the retries. A Go pool drains on shutdown, and failed runs queue their webhooks in the same transaction.

examples.title: The queue: a one-statement SKIP LOCKED claim, a lease that outlives its worker, and a fenced finish

annotations.note: Declared where it is used: claim needs only QueryRow, which both a pool and a transaction have. The transaction is how this run holds w1's claim open while w2 claims.

The claim is one autocommitted statement: the subquery picks and locks a row, the UPDATE marks it running. The row lock lasts only for this statement; afterwards the lease in run_after keeps other workers away, and no transaction or connection stays open while the job runs.

run_after answers one question for every state: when may a worker take this job next? For a queued job it is the due time or the next retry; a claim sets it to the end of the lease, so a running job whose worker died becomes claimable again by itself, with no reaper. The lease token is new for every claim: a fencing token.

SKIP LOCKED: a claim passes over a row another claim is taking at this moment instead of waiting for that transaction to end. The docs call the resulting view of the table inconsistent, which a queue doesn't mind: any due job will do. The ORDER BY is the jobs_due index's order, so the claim reads that index from the start.
The fence. Every update after the claim names the lease token; zero rows means a later claim holds the job now, and the caller learns it as ErrLeaseLost and drops its result.

w1's claim is still uncommitted when w2 claims on another connection. w2 skips the row w1 has locked and gets chat at once; with plain FOR UPDATE it would wait for w1's commit, and claims would run one at a time.

w1 stops answering (a crash, a killed process, a frozen VM). Nothing notices: at 06:03:30 the lease still keeps everyone away, at 06:04:31 it has run out and the next claim gets ci back. The dead worker's attempt counts: this is attempt 2.
w1 resumes and reports success; the fence refuses it. w3, which holds the lease, finishes normally.

examples.title: The outbox: a failed run and its webhook deliveries commit together, or not at all

annotations.note: Enqueue is an INSERT inside the caller's transaction. A committed failed run always has its webhooks queued, and a rolled-back one never sends any. Step 10 published after the commit, so a crash in between lost the event.

The event is marshaled once, with its id, and stored as a string inside the payload. As a nested jsonb object it would come back with its keys reordered (jsonb doesn't keep key order); the string keeps the exact bytes that every attempt sends and signs.
One job per subscribed webhook, written by one INSERT ... SELECT: each receiver gets its own attempts, schedule and failure, so a dead chat server doesn't hold back the CI notification.
pgx.BeginFunc commits when the function returns nil and rolls back when it returns an error. Here a later step fails, and the second run takes its two deliveries with it.
One run, two jobs, and one event id between them: two deliveries of the same event, which receivers deduplicate on.

examples.title: A worker pool that drains on SIGTERM and gives back what it couldn't finish

annotations.note: Two contexts. stop is the signal: once it is canceled, no worker claims again. jobs is what running work sees; it is canceled only when the drain deadline passes, so a job that can finish in time does. context.WithoutCancel and context.AfterFunc are both Go 1.21.
sync.WaitGroup.Go (Go 1.25) starts a worker and counts it, so Wait returns when every worker has stopped.
Claim, run, claim again; when nothing is due, wait a moment. TraceLite polls every second; go.services.listen-notify shows how a NOTIFY could wake the workers instead.

The claim runs on jobs, not on stop: a claim already sent when the signal arrives may have committed in the database, and cancelling it could leave a job leased to a worker that never learns it got one.
pg_sleep stands in for step 8's report query. When the drain deadline cancels jobs, pgx cancels the running query.

A finished job is done. A job interrupted by shutdown is released: queued again at once, with its attempt given back, because a deploy is not the job's fault and shouldn't use up one of its six tries or wait for a lease to run out. Any other error is a retry (see How it works).
The outcome gets its own context: after the drain deadline the job's context is canceled, and an UPDATE sent with it would fail before reaching the database, leaving the job leased to nobody.
A background loop has nobody to return an error to, so it logs it. An ignored error here once hid a broken heartbeat in an earlier version of this step.

In cmd/tracelite this context comes from signal.NotifyContext. Here the "signal" is a timeout 100 ms in, when both workers have sent their claims: Raporlama (0.3 s) finishes inside the 700 ms drain, Ödeme (1.5 s) doesn't and is released, and Arşiv is never claimed. The next process finds both in the table and runs them.

examples.title: The finished report: 409 until it is done, then a download with Content-Length and ranges

annotations.note: A malformed id parses to the zero UUID, which matches no job: 404, as for any unknown path id.
Unknown job, or not a report: 404. A report that isn't done yet: 409 with the conflict problem type, whose detail tells the client what to do instead.

Step 8 had to stream and abort on failure. A finished file can be served properly: http.ServeContent sets Content-Length, takes the Content-Type from the name's extension, sends Last-Modified, answers Range requests with 206 and conditional requests with 304. The file name rule is step 8's.
A done report, as a worker leaves it: the file in result, stored by the same fenced UPDATE that marks the job done, so a worker that lost its lease can't publish a stale file.

A range from byte 29 to the end: the reply is 206 with Content-Range, which is how a download manager resumes a broken download. Content-Length counts bytes: the file has 75 characters and 76 bytes, because Ö takes two.

use_cases: Report and export generation that takes longer than a request should: queue it, answer 202, let the browser poll and download the finished file
Outbound webhooks and e-mail: queued in the same transaction as the change that triggers them (an outbox), delivered with retries over hours
Any slow, retryable task a request triggers (an import, thumbnails, e-mail), where the user can be told "queued" and come back later
A single-binary deployment with one PostgreSQL and no broker, where adding Redis or RabbitMQ would double the operational surface
strengths: Jobs commit and roll back with the data that caused them; with a broker, the message and the database write are two systems that can disagree after a crash
The queue is queryable with SQL: what is stuck, what failed and why, how many retries a receiver needed, with no extra tooling
SKIP LOCKED lets any number of workers in any number of processes claim concurrently without blocking each other or taking the same job
Leases and fencing make worker crashes boring: the job comes back by itself, and a late finisher can't overwrite its successor
weaknesses: Every claim, heartbeat and finish is a write: thousands of jobs per second would churn the table and its index, where a broker would not care
Polling adds up to a poll interval of latency and some idle queries; LISTEN/NOTIFY wake-ups remove the latency at the cost of a dedicated connection
Delivery is at least once: a worker that dies after a webhook POST but before finishing sends it again, so receivers must deduplicate
Done rows accumulate, including report files in bytea; a cleanup job and a retention rule are part of the design, not an afterthought

pitfalls.title: Holding a transaction open for the whole job
pitfalls.detail: Claiming with FOR UPDATE inside a transaction that lasts until the job ends also survives crashes (the lock dies with the connection), but it pins one connection per running job and keeps a transaction open for minutes, which holds back vacuum. Claim and commit; let the lease do the rest.

pitfalls.title: Finishing without the lease token
pitfalls.detail: UPDATE jobs SET state = 'done' WHERE id = $1 lets a worker that lost its lease overwrite the successor's result or mark a retried job done. Every update after the claim must say AND lease_token = $2 and check the row count.
pitfalls.bad: UPDATE jobs SET state = 'done' WHERE id = $1
pitfalls.good: UPDATE jobs SET state = 'done', lease_token = NULL WHERE id = $1 AND lease_token = $2 -- 0 rows: lease lost

pitfalls.title: Publishing after the commit instead of in it
pitfalls.detail: Calling the webhook dispatcher after tx.Commit loses the event if the process dies in between, and calling it before the commit sends events for runs that then roll back. Insert the job inside the transaction.

pitfalls.title: Recording the outcome with the canceled context
pitfalls.detail: After the drain deadline the job's context is canceled, and pgx returns at once without sending the UPDATE. The job then stays leased until the lease expires. Write the outcome with context.WithoutCancel plus a short timeout.

pitfalls.title: A lease shorter than the job, with no heartbeat
pitfalls.detail: If a report can run longer than the lease, another worker claims it while it runs, and again after that. Extend the lease periodically (every third of it) and stop the work if the extension finds the lease gone.

quiz.q: A worker claims a webhook job, posts it, and is killed before it can record the result. What happens?
options: When the lease runs out, another worker claims it and posts the event again, with the same event id
PostgreSQL rolls the claim back when the connection drops
quiz.why: The claim committed, so nothing rolls back. run_after holds the lease's end; after it, the claim query sees a due job. Receivers deduplicate on the event id.

quiz.q: Why does the claim use FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED rather than plain FOR UPDATE?
options: SKIP LOCKED is faster on small tables
So concurrent claims pass over a row being claimed instead of waiting for that claim's transaction to end
Plain FOR UPDATE can't be used with LIMIT
quiz.why: With plain FOR UPDATE every claim queues behind the one in progress; SKIP LOCKED gives each claimer a different due row at once.

quiz.q: SIGTERM arrives while a report has 3 minutes left and the drain is 20 seconds. What does TraceLite do?
options: Stops claiming, cancels the report after 20 seconds and releases it so the next process runs it at once
quiz.why: The drain bounds shutdown; Release puts the job back with run_after now and returns its attempt, because the interruption isn't the job's fault.

quiz.q: A failed run is recorded in a transaction that later rolls back. How many webhook deliveries are queued?
quiz.why: The job rows were inserted in the same transaction as the run (the outbox), so they roll back with it.

further_reading.title: PostgreSQL docs: SELECT, the locking clause (SKIP LOCKED)
PostgreSQL docs: JSON types (jsonb doesn't keep key order)

body: ## Concept Some work doesn't belong in a request: a traceability report for a large project takes minutes, and a webhook receiver may be down for hours. Step 8 streamed the report while the browser waited; step 10 retried webhooks in memory for a few seconds. Both are lost when TraceLite restarts. Step 11 turns that work into rows. A **job** is a row in `jobs` with a `kind`, a `payload`, a `state` and a time, `run_after`, before which no one may take it. - **Enqueue** = `INSERT`, inside the transaction that made the work necessary. A failed test run and its webhook deliveries commit together: the **outbox** pattern. - **Claim** = one `UPDATE … WHERE id = (SELECT … FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED)`. Concurrent workers, in one process or several, each get a different job and never wait for each other. - **Lease**: the claim sets `run_after` to the end of a lease and a fresh `lease_token`. If the worker dies, the lease runs out and the job is due again. A worker still alive extends it with a heartbeat. Every later update must present the token (fencing). - **Retry**: a failed attempt puts the job back with `run_after` further in the future (1 min, 5 min, 30 min, 2 h, 6 h, plus jitter); after the sixth attempt it is `failed`, with `last_error` kept. - **Shutdown**: on SIGTERM the pool stops claiming, lets running jobs finish within a drain period, cancels the rest through their context and releases them for the next process. The report endpoint becomes asynchronous: `POST` queues a job and answers **202 Accepted**, the browser polls the job, and the finished file is served with a real `Content-Length` and range support. ## Coming from C/C++/Java/Python/JS - **Python/Celery, Ruby/Sidekiq, Node/BullMQ**: the same model (a queue, workers, retries with backoff, a dead state) on Redis or RabbitMQ. Enqueuing there is a second system: the task can be sent for a transaction that then rolls back, or lost when the process dies between commit and send. Here the queue is in the same database, so the job commits with the data. Celery's `acks_late` plus `visibility_timeout` is this lesson's lease. - **Java**: Quartz's JDBC job store and db-scheduler also keep jobs in tables, but claim them differently. db-scheduler's default `fetch` strategy claims with an optimistic `UPDATE … WHERE … AND version = ?`; its `lock-and-fetch` strategy uses `SELECT … FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED`, as this step does. Quartz moves a trigger from WAITING to ACQUIRED with a conditional `UPDATE`, and a clustered Quartz serializes acquiring and firing with `SELECT … FOR UPDATE` on one row of its `LOCKS` table: a cluster-wide mutex, not a lock per job (db-scheduler's README and `JdbcTaskRepository.pick`; Quartz's JobStoreTX configuration docs and `JobStoreSupport`). Spring's `@Async` is an in-memory pool, closer to step 10's dispatcher, and loses its work on restart. Graceful shutdown in Spring is a property; here it is two contexts. - **AWS SQS**: `run_after` is SQS's visibility timeout, `attempts` its receive count, and `failed` its dead-letter queue. The fencing token is what SQS's receipt handle does: a delete with an old handle doesn't remove a message someone else received. - **C/C++**: a thread pool over a shared work list, except that the list survives the process and the lock is a row lock taken for one statement. ## How it works `migrations/004_jobs.sql`; the examples create only the columns they use: ```sql -- +goose Up CREATE TABLE jobs ( id uuid PRIMARY KEY DEFAULT uuidv7(), project_id uuid NOT NULL REFERENCES projects ON DELETE CASCADE, kind text NOT NULL CONSTRAINT jobs_kind_valid CHECK (kind IN ('report', 'webhook')), payload jsonb NOT NULL DEFAULT '{}', state text NOT NULL DEFAULT 'queued' CONSTRAINT jobs_state_valid CHECK (state IN ('queued', 'running', 'done', 'failed')), attempts integer NOT NULL DEFAULT 0, run_after timestamptz NOT NULL DEFAULT now(), -- no claim before this; a claim moves it to the lease's end lease_token uuid, -- new for every claim; finishing requires it last_error text NOT NULL DEFAULT '', result bytea, -- a finished report's file created_at timestamptz NOT NULL DEFAULT now(), finished_at timestamptz ); CREATE INDEX jobs_due ON jobs (run_after, id) WHERE state IN ('queued', 'running'); CREATE INDEX jobs_project ON jobs (project_id, created_at DESC); ``` One table for every kind of background work: the state, the attempts and the last error are columns anyone can query, unlike a queue that lives in a goroutine. `jobs_due` is a partial index over open jobs only, so done and failed rows pile up without slowing the claim; its order is the claim's `ORDER BY`, so the claim reads it from the start and stops at the first row it can lock. New endpoints in `openapi.yaml`: ```yaml /api/projects/{projectId}/traceability-report-jobs: parameters: [{ $ref: "#/components/parameters/ProjectId" }] post: operationId: queueTraceabilityReport responses: "202": description: Queued; poll the job named by Location headers: { Location: { schema: { type: string } } } content: { application/json: { schema: { $ref: "#/components/schemas/Job" } } } "404": { $ref: "#/components/responses/Problem" } /api/jobs/{jobId}: parameters: [{ $ref: "#/components/parameters/JobId" }] get: operationId: getJob responses: "200": { description: The job, content: { application/json: { schema: { $ref: "#/components/schemas/Job" } } } } "404": { $ref: "#/components/responses/Problem" } /api/jobs/{jobId}/file: parameters: [{ $ref: "#/components/parameters/JobId" }] get: operationId: getJobFile description: A finished report (step 8's TraceabilityReport); supports Range. responses: "200": { description: The file, headers: { Content-Disposition: { schema: { type: string } } } } "206": { description: The requested byte range } "404": { $ref: "#/components/responses/Problem" } "409": { $ref: "#/components/responses/Problem" } # not done yet # components.parameters: JobId: { name: jobId, in: path, required: true, schema: { type: string, format: uuid } } # components.schemas: Job: type: object required: [id, kind, state, attempts, lastError, createdAt, finishedAt] properties: id: { type: string, format: uuid } kind: { type: string, enum: [report, webhook] } state: { type: string, enum: [queued, running, done, failed] } attempts: { type: integer, minimum: 0 } lastError: { type: string } createdAt: { type: string, format: date-time } finishedAt: { type: [string, "null"], format: date-time } ``` A job's life: ```mermaid stateDiagram-v2 [*] --> queued: INSERT (in the caller's transaction) queued --> running: claim (SKIP LOCKED), run_after = lease end running --> running: heartbeat extends the lease running --> done: handler ok (fenced UPDATE, result stored) running --> queued: retryable error, run_after = now + backoff running --> queued: shutdown: released, attempt given back running --> running: lease expired, claimed by another worker running --> failed: permanent error, or the sixth attempt failed ``` The code lives in a new package, `internal/jobs`: `Queue` (claim, extend, finish, release, plus `Enqueue(ctx, tx, …)` taking the caller's transaction) and `Pool`. Handlers are registered by kind: `report` (step 8's query, written into `result`) and `webhook` (one POST per attempt, signed as in step 10; the in-memory retry loop of step 10 is gone, because each claim is one attempt). Settings in `cmd/tracelite`: 4 workers, a poll every second, a 2-minute lease with a heartbeat every 40 s, a 20 s drain. What `Finish` writes, always fenced with `AND lease_token = $2` as in example 1: - The handler returned nil: `done`, with `finished_at`, and for a report the file in `result`, in the same UPDATE. - It returned a `Permanent` error (webhooks: a 4xx other than 410 and 429): `failed`, with `last_error`. Found with `errors.AsType[Permanent](err)` (Go 1.26). - Any other error (webhooks: 429, 5xx, a timeout): `queued` again with `run_after = now + schedule[attempts-1]`, where the schedule is 1 min, 5 min, 30 min, 2 h, 6 h, plus up to 10% jitter; after the sixth attempt, `failed`, keeping `last_error` for the UI. That is about nine hours in all, which covers a receiver's bad night but not a weekend. Unlike step 10's full jitter, a retry here must not come earlier than the schedule says; the spread only keeps a backlog from reaching a receiver in one burst when it comes back. - The pool is shutting down (example 3): released. While a handler runs, a heartbeat extends the lease every third of it (`UPDATE jobs SET run_after = $3 WHERE id = $1 AND lease_token = $2`). A report that takes longer than one lease keeps it; without the heartbeat another worker would claim the running report every two minutes. When the extension finds zero rows, the lease is lost and the heartbeat cancels the handler's context. Log its errors: an ignored error once hid a heartbeat that failed on every tick. The report endpoint answers before any work is done. RFC 9110's 202 Accepted means the request is valid and will be processed, not that it has been; `Location` names the job, and the body is the job as it stands, so the first poll is already answered: ```go mux.HandleFunc("POST /api/projects/{projectId}/traceability-report-jobs", func(w http.ResponseWriter, r *http.Request) { project, _ := uuid.Parse(r.PathValue("projectId")) // a malformed id finds no project var j Job // the Job schema below, json tags in camelCase err := db.QueryRow(r.Context(), `INSERT INTO jobs (project_id, kind) SELECT id, 'report' FROM projects WHERE id = $1 RETURNING id, kind, state, attempts, last_error, created_at, finished_at`, project). Scan(&j.ID, &j.Kind, &j.State, &j.Attempts, &j.LastError, &j.CreatedAt, &j.FinishedAt) if errors.Is(err, pgx.ErrNoRows) { err = store.ErrNotFound // no such project } if err != nil { writeError(w, err) // step 4's: ErrNotFound is a 404, anything else a 500 return } j.CreatedAt = j.CreatedAt.UTC() w.Header().Set("Location", "/api/jobs/"+j.ID.String()) w.Header().Set("Content-Type", "application/json") w.WriteHeader(http.StatusAccepted) json.MarshalWrite(w, j) }) ``` Between the 202 and the work, TraceLite could be restarted, upgraded or switched off overnight. The request is a row in `jobs`, so the next process does it. Example 4 serves the finished file. Shutdown order in `main`: first `http.Server.Shutdown` (a request in flight may still enqueue), then the pool's drain, then the step 9 listener, then the database pool. Keep the sum under the supervisor's patience: `docker stop` waits 10 s by default before SIGKILL, systemd 90 s. In the browser, the report button posts, then polls the job until it ends, then offers the file as a plain link (TanStack Query v5 accepts a function for `refetchInterval`): ```tsx const job = useQuery({ queryKey: ["jobs", jobId], queryFn: () => request(Job, `/api/jobs/${jobId}`), refetchInterval: (q) => q.state.data?.state === "queued" || q.state.data?.state === "running" ? 1000 : false, }); // done: Raporu indir ``` ## Design notes **PostgreSQL as the queue.** TraceLite already runs one database and one binary; a broker would double what must be installed, backed up and monitored on a customer's machine. A jobs table handles hundreds of jobs a minute without strain, and its real advantage is transactional: enqueueing commits with the data. The trade-off reverses at high volume (thousands per second, many consumers), where claims and heartbeats become write load and a broker earns its place (go.services.grpc-brokers). **Leases rather than long transactions.** Holding the row lock for the whole job would also return a crashed worker's job (the lock dies with its connection), but it ties up a pooled connection and an open transaction per running job, for minutes. The lease costs two extra columns and a heartbeat, and lets a job outlive any one connection. **At least once, made harmless.** No queue can guarantee that a POST happened exactly once: a worker can die after the receiver processed the event and before the job is marked done. TraceLite redelivers with the same event id (step 10), and receivers deduplicate. Effects inside the database are better off: the report is written by the same fenced statement that marks the job done, so it is stored once. **Time comes from Go.** The queue reads its clock from a `now func() time.Time` (example 1 passes the time in and moves it by hand; example 3 and `cmd/tracelite` use `time.Now`). Several TraceLite processes would then need synchronized clocks, which NTP gives to well within the one-minute scale of leases and retries. Using the database's `now()` instead would give one clock and lose the testability. **Housekeeping.** Once a day the pool deletes done and failed jobs older than 30 days, and with them their report files; the UI says how long a report stays downloadable. A second POST while a report is still queued creates a second job; a partial unique index on `(project_id) WHERE kind = 'report' AND state IN ('queued', 'running')` would prevent that, at the price of one more rule to explain.

expected.queue:
w1 claimed ci and w2 claimed chat without waiting for w1
06:03:30 claim: no rows in result set
06:04:31 w3 claimed ci attempt 2
w1 comes back, finishes: lease lost: the job was claimed again | w3 finishes: <nil>
expected.outbox:
run 1 committed: <nil>
run 2 rolled back: a later statement failed
test runs: 1, delivery jobs: 2, event ids among them: 1
expected.workers:
Ödeme     queued attempts 0 'interrupted by shutdown'
Raporlama done   attempts 1 ''
Arşiv     queued attempts 0 ''
